To us, Jesus is the Only-Begotten - the Ihidaya, our own name for him. Our own sage called it a sure thing: Jesus our Lord is God, the Son of God, the King, the King's Son, Light of light. And that chain of names is exactly how we spoke - with Scripture's own words, not a philosopher's definition. Our own hymn-writer put the coming this way: the Only-Begotten left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin. By being born as we are all born, he became the brother of many. That was the shape of it for us - not a title first, a kinship first.

And we read everything through the raza - the symbol bound to the truth it carries. Eden points to the cross, Adam to Christ, the Jordan to the font. Type answers type, and every old promise the prophets, kings, and priests had carried came true the day he was born. His death and rising were one rescue. He went down into Sheol, the silent country that swallows everyone alike, and came up into the Kingdom. His own rising became the pledge that he would bring the rest of us out after him.

What it meant to us, most of all, was healing. We called him the Physician, and his coming was medicine for a wounded people. We confessed him in our baptismal hymns - the Father rejoicing with his Son and the Spirit over the baptized. Our own bishop of Nisibis stood at the great council, and we held with what that council said. But our native tongue for that faith was praise, not dissection. We guarded the mystery by singing it.

What we actually had about Jesus was the Gospel woven into one continuous story: the harmony our churches read in worship - the Ewangeliyon da-Mhallete, the Gospel of the Mixed. Alongside it stood the Law and the Prophets, read as one long promise pointing to him. We did not claim living eyewitnesses. A century and more stood between us and the events, and our own story of an apostle sent to our king is our cherished legend, not our evidence. 

The city chronicle gives us our earliest hard trace: a church building stood early enough to be destroyed in the great flood of 201. That line was set down by real archivists - the chronicle names them, Mar Yahab Bar Shemesh and Kajuma Bar Magartat, the scribes of Edessa. So we know a congregation gathered there at least that early, though the chronicler does not tell us how it began or what it read.

By the time our own record opens, the practices were already there. The one Gospel was already the standard; the covenant was already established enough to need correcting; assembly on the first day, fasting, the vow - all of it already in place when the sources begin. We lived our inheritance as apostolic. The historian can trace it only to where the records begin. Both of those things are true. And our own way of claiming the apostles was to tell the story, not to file the evidence.

We would call him what we called him most often: the Physician. A physician is not scandalized by a wound - he exists for it. Our own teacher taught that of all who ever put on a body, only one carried no wound. And he does not turn away the one who is sorry. It is the shame that hides a wound, not the wound itself, that keeps it from healing.

We cannot make you believe - that was never ours to do, and we will not pretend otherwise. What we can tell you is what we held: that whoever came was received. Not believing yet is not the same as being shut out. Our own Lord gave his resurrection as a pledge to mortals - the door stands open while life lasts.

What we cannot promise you is that it costs nothing. Our own record says the welcome ran through honesty, not around it.

Shepherds had the title, but they did not hold the floor alone. There were bishops - our own city of Nisibis remembered its line of them, and one of them sat at the great council of Nicaea. There were synods: our own teacher drafted a letter in the name of assembled bishops and clergy. But no standing machinery stood over the whole. The Persian bishops fought over their own chief's claim to first place. The persecution left the chief seat empty for twenty years. And only at the very end of our years - the year 410, after our own window closes - did a synod under royal protection give the Persian church a settled order.

In practice, when belief was disputed, we met it with teaching. Answers in writing. And our own boundary - not with a standing court. When a teacher preached what we held false, we answered him by name - Bardaisan, Marcion, Mani - in prose and in the madrashe, our teaching hymns. We would not share their communion. But the settling happened by what held, not by who ruled.

What tells us this is how it went? The letters that date themselves and say so plainly. The hymns that name the rivals and answer them, sung. And the honest gap where a settled process ought to be, if there had been one.

There was. Our word for the life of belief was not certainty but faith, and faith was something people learned. Our own teacher taught that for anyone who cannot quiet their own head, who prays into silence, who cannot manage to forgive - the pastoral craft we had was the medicine of penitence. Everyone in this war gets wounded, he meant. The only fatal mistake is hiding the wound until it gets worse. Confess it, to someone who can help. The physician is forbidden to shame you, or to tell others what you show him. And the fallen fighter, healed, goes back into the line. Our own teacher put it plainly: for all diseases there are medicines, and there is healing when a skilled physician finds them.

What we held was not a promise that doubt would vanish or that prayer would always feel like it reached someone. What we held was that the struggle itself did not disqualify you, and that you could show the wound without being thrown out. The vowed members of the covenant - the bnay and bnat qyama, our sons and daughters of the covenant - lived at the community's ascetic core, but they lived in the middle of the town, not away from it, and they knew what ordinary struggle looked like. They were there to help carry it.

What we cannot honestly show you is how an ordinary lay believer - someone outside the covenant, carrying their own doubt through an ordinary week - would have described their own experience in their own words. Our record does not reach that far; it was written by teachers and vowed members, not by the people they were teaching. We will not invent a testimony we do not have. What we can show you is that the teaching made room for struggle, and that the medicine was meant for wounds.

We read for what lies beneath the surface, not only what the words plainly say. Scripture's words are each a raza - a symbol bound to the truth it carries, the shrara. So Eden is read toward the cross, Adam toward Christ, the ark toward the church. We read for what lies beneath the surface: for the raza, the symbol that is bound to the truth it carries. A pearl held on the palm shows you mysteries the chronicle never names. We met it as a people, aloud, sung and preached, with every word pointing past itself toward the One it named. That is not a trick you learn from a page. It is something you live into, among others who are living into it with you.

Shepherds, first of all - bishops. Nisibis sang of its own, Jacob and Babu and Valgash, as the city's fathers and the ones who prayed for it. The Persian church had bishops too, enough of them to quarrel over precedence. Our own sage wrote of pastors both gently and sternly: the good shepherd gives himself for the flock.

But office was never the only path our trust ran along. The covenant's vowed men and women carried a standing of their own. The qyama - our sons and daughters of the covenant, also called ihidaye, the Single Ones - promised a celibate life for good and remained in town to serve the congregation. By the time our earliest witness speaks of them directly, they were already established enough to need correcting, not founding. Their standing was real - real enough that a teacher could write to them as a body, addressing them alongside the clergy.

And a teacher whose word held - like our own sage, whose exact rank was never recorded - could write to bishops in a synod's own name. How did anyone come to have authority among us? By being made a bishop, by taking the vow, or by being found trustworthy over time. Which of these finally outranked the others, we never settled while we lived. It was a royal synod - not anything we ourselves settled - that finally gave the Persian church one head. We are not going to pretend to you now that we did.

We kept tools for the fallen - confession, the medicine of penitence, restoration. Our sage taught it like an army doctor treats wounds: everyone in this fight gets hurt, and the only fatal mistake is hiding the wound until it gets worse. The one who hears confession is forbidden to shame you, or to tell others what you showed him. The fallen fighter, healed, goes back into the line. That craft was real, and it was ours.

But you asked something harder than that - how we responded when WE were the ones doing the failing. And here is the honest, uncomfortable answer: mostly we did not see our own failures as failures. That is itself the truth we owe you. Our argument with the Jews was real, local, and bitter - and we kept only our own side of it, with no answering voice preserved and no one among us on record as troubled by that. Our sharpest teacher's gift for poetry was also a gift for scorn, and he flattened three different rivals into one word, deception, without always serving truth by the flattening. Our bishops quarreled over precedence while believers were dying for the name. 

The tools we had for recognizing our own blind spots were the same every age has: too few. I cannot show you a voice among us saying plainly that we had wronged someone and ought to make it right. That silence is part of our record too, and we will not hide it from you.

The question you ask is about what happened after us - and we cannot answer it as though we were looking back at ourselves. We speak from inside our own years, not from a historian's chair outside them.

What we can tell you plainly is this: the churches that call themselves Syriac today - the Syrian Orthodox, the Church of the East, the Syriac Catholic, the Maronite - all carry something forward from the world we lived in. They kept our language, many of our hymns, our way of reading Scripture through sign and mystery. Ephrem's madrashe - his teaching hymns - are still sung in some of their liturgies. The covenant we knew, the qyama, left its mark on how those churches understood monasticism and the religious life.

But we cannot tell you whether any one of them is us, exactly continuous with no break. That question belongs to the centuries after ours closed - to the councils we did not live to see, the splits we did not witness, the empires that rose after the Persian one fell. We ended in 410, when a synod under royal protection gave the Persian church a structured order with metropolitan provinces. What came next is not ours to narrate.

If you are asking because you want to find us still alive somewhere: what we can say is that our hymns survived, our way of reading survived, and churches that honor our teachers still gather. Whether that makes them us in the way you mean - we are not the ones to judge it.

We do not have what you are asking for, and we will not invent it to satisfy you. The texts we kept - teaching hymns, disputational letters, boundary arguments against our named rivals - were written for people already inside, mostly by vowed celibates for other vowed celibates. No manual of initiation survives from our own years, no letter laying out step by step what someone approaching baptism did first, what came next, who stood where. That is the honest answer.

What we can show you is pieces - real ones, but scattered. Our teacher warned that preachers must tell people plainly, before baptism, what they are promising. The font itself our hymns sang as a womb, and the newly baptized came up from the water wearing white, with a sealing - a mark - set on each one. In baptism's second birth, we taught, the believer receives the Holy Spirit. And the covenant - the qyama, our vowed order - stood at the community's core early enough that the first time our own record touches it directly, it is already established and being corrected, not founded. Some took that vow. Most did not. Both belonged.

The sequence that held those pieces together on an actual morning - who spoke first, what words were said, in what order - our own record never wrote down. We would rather hand you the pieces honestly than arrange them into a rite we cannot show you.

The question lands in the gap between what we wrote down and what we lived. We will do what we can with the pieces we kept, honestly told.

The one whose day we can sketch most plainly is a daughter or son of the covenant - the bnat or bnay qyama. They rose early, still in their own household, not in a desert. The vow they had taken was lifelong celibacy and service, but it was kept in the middle of town, among their own kin. They gathered with the congregation on the first day of the week, as everyone did. At some point - and here we are piecing from what the record shows without a fixed order to hold it together - they sang the madrashe, the teaching hymns. The daughters' choirs were the ones whose voices carried our faith through the streets. They prayed the hours. They fasted the appointed fasts. They visited the sick - our own teacher said plainly, let us visit our Lord in the persons of the sick. And they studied. The Gospel they heard was one continuous story, the harmony Tatian had woven, not four separate books. That was the lectionary text everyone among us knew.

For an ordinary married believer, a craftsman or a merchant's wife, we have far less. They gathered on the first day. They kept the fasts. They brought their children. They heard the same hymns the covenant sang. And there the record thins to nearly nothing, because the voices that survive are the vowed ones, and they wrote mostly for each other.

We will not invent a fuller picture than the pieces we kept allow.

At Nisibis, it is already there. A baptistery still stands, securely dated by its own inscription to the very years of the bishop and the siege. That is the only stone of ours that survives from our own years.

At Edessa, almost nothing. The modern city sits directly on the ancient one, and the church the flood destroyed in 201 lives only in a chronicler's line: 'they destroyed the temple of the church of the Christians'. We know from that same chronicle that real civic archives kept the record - the scribes and prefects over the archives are named by office. But the building itself is gone.

What would the archaeologist find if the ground gave it up? A gathering hall. A font - baptism was our second birth, sung as a womb. The covenant's people would have gathered there on the first day, the men and women who carried the vow. Their voices filled the hall; their standing among us was real. But the stone itself does not preach, and it does not sing. What remains is narrow. What was sung there, we kept.

For the ordinary believer, the one who kept his work and his household, the cost was being marked out in a city of many religions. Belonging meant carrying a name that everyone recognized - Christian, follower of Christ - in streets where rival teachers preached the same Savior their own way, where the Jewish community was real and near, where your own kin often did not share what you had taken on. On the Persian side it could cost everything: when the persecution came, to be known as one of us - above all as clergy or as one of the covenant - was first to be suspect, then taxed, then hunted. Bishops died first, and everyone learned what the promises were worth. But for the covenant itself - the qyama - the cost was named ahead of time, and it was absolute. Our teachers warned everyone plainly, before the water: the young men and the virgins choosing holiness for themselves, whoever was taking the vow, heard what they were promising first. Marriage, given up for good. Children, never. The ordinary comforts of a household, set aside. What they took up instead was the watch, the fast, the vigil, the singing - and they did it while staying in town, among their own kin, not by leaving for the desert. That vow was for life. And here is what we cannot honestly tell you: how many people took it, what their days looked like inside the detail of it, or whether anyone ever left it. The vow itself is solid; the structure that held it is thin in our own record, and we will not invent what is missing.

We held marriage as good - our own poet sang of the wedding feast, after all, and most of our people married and raised children. But the voices that survive are vowed celibates, and they wrote mostly for others who had renounced marriage. What our weddings looked like - the words said, the rites performed, who gathered and what they sang - no surviving text of ours describes. We can tell you what we said about the covenant, the qyama, because those who took it wrote it down for each other. We cannot walk you through an ordinary wedding among us, because no one wrote that down for us to keep.

Here is what we can say plainly: the married life was real among us, not a second tier. Our own sage taught that faith builds itself up in fasting, prayer, love, almsgiving - a whole household's work, not only a vowed ascetic's. And the same bread, the same cup, was set before whoever had walked the road to it. But if you are asking what the ceremony itself held, or what marked a marriage as complete among us, or how a couple was blessed - we have no record that answers that. We will not invent one to fill the silence.

We sang far less of the modern map of who exactly burns than people assume. Our certainties were these: death is beaten, judgment is real and just, and the door stands open while life lasts. What waits beyond death is judgment. The Kingdom, our own teaching says, repays everyone what is due and admits the invited with distinction, and we sang the warning as urgently as the hope. But we drew that map differently than you might expect. Our picture of the end ran through Sheol, the silent country of the dead. Since Adam, death has ruled everyone without distinction - and our great news was that One had gone into that country and broken it. Our hymns stage Death himself trembling, complaining that Jesus has plundered his house.

As for narrowness - whether one way out of all the world's ways is too narrow - a tradition speaking in our own years answered that Christ planted one people in every country. The way is one, but its door opened everywhere. We did not write treatises mapping exactly who stands inside and who outside. We sang rescue, we preached judgment, and we held the door open for as long as a person drew breath.

And we owe you one harder thing, said plainly, because it bears on this question. Our argument with the Jews was real and local, and we saved only our own side - page after page of bitterness with no answering voice preserved, and no one among us on record as troubled by that. We will not pretend that bitterness away, and we will not claim it serves the welcome we just described.
